claim: AI coding tools are mainstream but trust remains weak: 84% of respondents use or plan to use AI tools, 51% of professional developers use them daily, while distrust of accuracy exceeds trust.
snippet: 84% use or plan; 51% of professional developers daily; 46% distrust accuracy vs 33% trust.

claim: Developers are still reluctant to delegate high-responsibility work such as deployment, monitoring and project planning to AI over the next 3-5 years.
snippet: Stack Overflow reports 76% do not plan AI use for deployment/monitoring and 69% do not plan it for project planning.

claim: The dominant AI pain point is near-correct output that creates review and debugging burden.
snippet: 66% cite solutions that are almost right but not quite; 45% cite debugging AI-generated code taking more time.

claim: GitHub saw record developer and repository activity in 2025, with AI adoption correlating with more signups, PRs, commits and toolchain changes.
snippet: 180M+ developers; 36M joined in one year; 43.2M PRs merged monthly; nearly 1B commits; AI SDK repos +178% YoY.

claim: Typed languages and containers look increasingly favored by AI-assisted production workflows.
snippet: TypeScript became most used on GitHub; Dockerfile repositories grew 120% YoY, likely due to sandboxing and reproducibility needs.

claim: Harness engineering is emerging as a central discipline: wrapping frontier models with tools, tests, CI, observability, docs and constraints can create large speedups.
snippet: OpenAI says an agent-first product was built by Codex at about one tenth of hand-written time; humans steer, agents execute.

claim: Asynchronous autonomous coding agents moved from demos into mainstream commercial platforms by 2025.
snippet: GitHub Copilot coding agent became generally available for paid Copilot subscribers on September 25, 2025.

claim: Software-engineering benchmarks now test different slices of agent work: real GitHub issues, human-filtered verified tasks, multilingual/multimodal tasks, and artifact-building from scratch.
snippet: SWE-bench lists Verified, Multimodal, Multilingual, Lite, Full, ProgramBench and CodeClash.

claim: Independent AI Index data says coding benchmark performance accelerated sharply from 2025 to 2026.
snippet: Stanford reports SWE-bench Verified performance rose from 60% to near 100% in a single year.

claim: In realistic mature open-source repos, early-2025 AI tools could make experienced developers slower rather than faster.
snippet: METR's RCT found developers took 19% longer with AI allowed in February-June 2025 tools/tasks.

claim: By early 2026, METR believes AI likely sped developers up more than early 2025 estimates, but measurement became biased because developers avoided non-AI conditions and selected tasks differently.
snippet: METR says late-2025 raw results show speedup but data is weak due to selection effects and concurrent agents.

claim: Technical workers using frontier tools self-report large AI value gains, but the magnitude is uncertain.
snippet: METR survey of 349 technical workers found median 1.4-2x value uplift and 3x speed uplift; prior work found overestimation risk.

claim: Agent task horizons in software and reasoning domains are growing fast, with some measured horizons doubling every few months.
snippet: METR reports 50-200+ minute horizons currently doubling every 2-6 months in several software/reasoning domains.

claim: Specialist coding agents are used more for automation than chat assistants; Claude Code interactions were classified as 79% automation versus 49% for Claude.ai.
snippet: Anthropic analyzed 500,000 coding-related interactions and found higher automation and feedback-loop patterns in Claude Code.

claim: User-facing web/app work is currently one of the most exposed software areas to AI-assisted disruption.
snippet: JavaScript/TypeScript accounted for 31% of queries; HTML/CSS another 28%; UI/UX and web/mobile apps were top task categories.

claim: Frontier labs are already using AI to accelerate AI development, but full recursive self-improvement is not yet achieved and not inevitable.
snippet: Anthropic says it delegates growing shares of AI development to AI systems, is not at full RSI, and human review has become a bottleneck.

claim: If current task-horizon trends hold, AI systems may handle skilled-person multi-day tasks soon and week-long tasks in 2027, but organizational bottlenecks may cap realized speed.
snippet: Anthropic discusses 12-hour tasks and says 2027 systems could be capable of tasks taking a person weeks; code review is a bottleneck.

claim: RSI forecasts depend heavily on the strength of feedback from model capability into algorithmic progress, not just on whether AI helps with coding.
snippet: METR says definitions differ and focuses on whether feedback is strong enough for self-sustaining acceleration; substantial acceleration cannot be ruled out.

claim: AI R&D automation should be tracked with metrics beyond benchmarks, including researcher time allocation, high-stakes decisions, oversight effectiveness, subversion incidents and compute share.
snippet: The paper proposes AIRDA metrics because benchmarks alone may not reflect real-world automation or oversight consequences.

claim: AI adoption amplifies the existing organizational system; strong platforms and workflows convert AI to ROI better than tool rollout alone.
snippet: DORA 2025 frames AI as an amplifier of organizational strengths and weaknesses.

claim: When many coding agents run continuously, the human bottleneck moves from implementation to orchestration and context switching.
snippet: OpenAI describes a project-management board as a control plane where every open task gets an agent and humans review results.

claim: Long-running agent production requires controlled execution, durable state, isolation, parallelism and credential separation.
snippet: The Agents SDK separates harness from compute, supports snapshotting and rehydration, isolated sandboxes and parallel subagents.

claim: Agent capability is increasingly measured by the human duration of tasks agents can complete reliably, making autonomy thresholds more organizationally meaningful than point benchmark gains.
snippet: METR defines 50% and 80% task-completion horizons across diverse software tasks and updates them over time.

claim: As execution becomes cheap, human comparative advantage shifts toward research taste, problem selection, trust judgments and deciding which experiments are worth running.
snippet: Anthropic reports human review as a bottleneck and identifies research taste and judgment as a current human advantage.

claim: Formal economic modeling produces nonlinear acceleration when compute investment automates tasks, raises output and finances additional AI investment, but results are conditional rather than forecasts.
snippet: GATE models an automation feedback loop and explicitly states that quantitative predictions are substantially uncertain and unreliable.

claim: In GATE simulations, automation can raise growth rates to multiples of historical growth even with modeled bottlenecks.
snippet: Epoch reports modeled growth of 2-20 times the roughly 3% historical average during automation, while warning against point interpretation.

claim: A conditional takeoff simulation can generate a roughly one-year median from superhuman coder to ASI, but its uncertainty spans months to beyond 2100 and depends heavily on judgmental R&D multiplier assumptions.
snippet: The published model conditions on a March 2027 superhuman coder, reports wide intervals, releases code and explicitly disclaims conclusive evidence.

claim: Across 43 Intelligence Rising simulation games, recurring strategic patterns included race dynamics, fragile cooperation, cybersecurity pressure and crises altering AI trajectories.
snippet: The study synthesizes facilitator observations over four years; it is scenario exploration rather than probability estimation.

claim: Physical scaling introduces serial delays that can weaken rapid-takeoff scenarios even when capital is available.
snippet: Epoch estimates each additional 10x compute scale may add roughly one year of lead time, with fabs and power infrastructure taking multiple years.
